identification.summary: Lace Tempest is Microsoft's name for a financially motivated threat actor, also tracked as DEV-0950, that Microsoft describes as a Clop ransomware affiliate [S1][S7]. Microsoft says its activity overlaps with FIN11 and TA505 [S1][S4]. The actor is associated with mass exploitation of internet-facing file-transfer and IT-management software in 2023 [S1][S3][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Earliest dated activity in the sources gathered: PaperCut exploitation as early as 2023-04-13, per Microsoft as reported by press [S1]. Microsoft reporting on earlier GoAnywhere and Raspberry Robin use is relayed secondhand [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Lace Tempest (financially motivated), formerly DEV-0950 [S7]. Press coverage ties the name to the Clop (Cl0p) extortion operation, but vendor cluster boundaries differ: Mandiant tracks MOVEit activity under its own designation and press notes FIN11/TA505 overlap, not identity [S1][S5]. One secondary source calls the actor an initial access broker while most call it a ransomware affiliate [S4]. Microsoft's Dec 2023 post says Sangria Tempest (FIN7) has cooperated with Lace Tempest in past intrusions; these are separate Microsoft clusters [S6].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered; Microsoft classifies the actor as financially motivated [S7].
attribution.confidence: Attributed by Microsoft to Lace Tempest for PaperCut (April 2023), MOVEit Transfer (May-June 2023) and SysAid (November 2023) exploitation, as relayed by press [S1][S3][S5]. The Clop link is Microsoft's characterization; some outlets describe it as likely rather than confirmed, and Clop separately claimed MOVEit responsibility [S2][S5]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and naming, relayed through press and vendor write-ups; Microsoft's own primary posts were not opened [S1][S3][S5][S7].

objectives: Financial gain through data theft, extortion and ransomware, with exploitation of widely deployed enterprise software to reach many victims [S1][S3][S5].

sectors: Organizations running exposed PaperCut print-management servers
Organizations running MOVEit Transfer (government, payroll/HR providers, private companies)
Organizations running SysAid on-premises IT service management
regions: Global; MOVEit victims reported in the US, Canada (Nova Scotia) and the UK (Zellis) [S5]
targeting.notes: Targeting is opportunistic and driven by which vulnerable product is internet-exposed rather than by a fixed sector. SysAid said to have over 5,000 customers [S3]. US government agencies were among MOVEit victims per press [S5].

capabilities.summary: Rapid exploitation of internet-facing enterprise software, including zero-days: PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 (unauthenticated RCE, CVSS 9.8) and CVE-2023-27351 [S1], MOVEit Transfer CVE-2023-34362 (SQL injection; LEMURLOOT web shell per Mandiant) [S5], and SysAid CVE-2023-47246 (path traversal) [S3][S4]. In the PaperCut intrusions Microsoft reported PowerShell delivery of a TrueBot DLL that tried to steal LSASS credentials and injected into conhost.exe, a Cobalt Strike Beacon, WMI lateral movement and exfiltration via MegaSync [S1]. In SysAid intrusions a WAR archive containing a web shell was placed in the Tomcat webroot, followed by MeshAgent and GraceWire [S3]. Microsoft says GraceWire is typically affiliated with Lace Tempest [S6]. Microsoft reported earlier use of GoAnywhere exploits and Raspberry Robin [S1].

campaigns.name: PaperCut server exploitation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft said Lace Tempest exploited CVE-2023-27350 and CVE-2023-27351 as early as 2023-04-13; PaperCut disclosed active exploitation on 2023-04-19. Chain: PowerShell, TrueBot DLL, Cobalt Strike, WMI, MegaSync. Microsoft separately saw LockBit deployments in some related intrusions [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: MOVEit Transfer mass exploitation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft attributed exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 to Lace Tempest. Mandiant reported earliest exploitation on 2023-05-27 and Progress advised on 2023-05-31; the LEMURLOOT web shell enabled data theft. Victims included Zellis, Nova Scotia and several US government agencies. Clop claimed responsibility to BleepingComputer [S5].

campaigns.name: SysAid zero-day exploitation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft detected exploitation of SysAid on-premises software and reported it to the vendor; SysAid learned of the zero-day on 2023-11-02 and patched CVE-2023-47246 in version 23.3.36 on 2023-11-08. Elastic reported exploitation as early as 2023-10-30. Intrusions used a web shell, MeshAgent and GraceWire [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: GraceWire in Sangria Tempest App Installer chains
campaigns.summary: Microsoft noted POWERTRASH loading NetSupport and GraceWire, malware typically affiliated with Lace Tempest, in Sangria Tempest (FIN7) activity, and that Sangria Tempest has cooperated with Lace Tempest before [S6].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercrime actor tracked by Microsoft as Lace Tempest (DEV-0950), described as a Clop affiliate with FIN11/TA505 overlap [S1][S7].
diamond.capability: Zero-day and n-day exploitation of PaperCut, MOVEit Transfer and SysAid; web shells; TrueBot, GraceWire, MeshAgent, Cobalt Strike; MegaSync exfiltration [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Exposed vulnerable servers used as initial access; specific C2 infrastructure is not documented in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Organizations running internet-facing PaperCut, MOVEit Transfer or SysAid servers, including government and downstream customers of service providers [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal extortion economy: data theft and ransom demands; no state direction stated [S7].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed enterprise file-transfer, print-management and IT-service-management applications with unauthenticated vulnerabilities [S1][S3][S5].

gaps: Microsoft's original Lace Tempest posts (PaperCut, SysAid, MOVEit attribution) could not be opened; claims are relayed by press and vendor write-ups. Validate wording against Microsoft primaries.
Microsoft's Defender monthly news item (reported as stating first SysAid attacks on 2023-10-27) was not opened; the date is not independently confirmed here.
Boundary between Lace Tempest, FIN11, TA505, Clop and Mandiant's MOVEit cluster is unresolved; overlap is not identity.
Press sources disagree on role (affiliate vs initial access broker) and some misprint the alias and CVE number.
Activity after 2023 (for example later Clop file-transfer campaigns) was not verified under the Lace Tempest name.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID, infrastructure indicators or victim-count figures specific to Lace Tempest were gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing file-transfer, print-management and IT-service-management servers are key terrain, especially those holding or bridging DoD-adjacent contractor and partner data [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2: The actor weaponizes newly disclosed or zero-day flaws within days, shrinking patch windows [S1][S3]. STEP 3: Pattern is exploit, web shell, loader (TrueBot/GraceWire/MeshAgent), Cobalt Strike, lateral movement, exfiltration, extortion [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is another mass-exploitation wave against a popular exposed enterprise application with data-theft extortion. MDCOA is the same technique against a defense-industrial-base managed file transfer or service-desk platform, exposing controlled data and disrupting operations. Candidate indicators: unexpected WAR/ASPX/JSP files in web roots, PowerShell spawning from print or service-desk services, conhost.exe injection, MeshAgent installs, MegaSync traffic [S1][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor advisories and KEV-style exploitation notices for file-transfer, print and ITSM platforms and push them to mission owners quickly. (2) Authorities: patching, isolation or take-down of exposed servers on mission networks needs pre-delegated decision authority since exploitation precedes patches. (3) Mission assurance: inventory these applications in the key cyber terrain list and know downstream dependencies and third-party hosting. (4) Coordination: notify DC3/DIB partners and service providers when exploited products are identified; ransomware-linked data theft may involve law enforcement and CISA channels.
